strengths: The orientation-resolved analysis reveals structured successes and failures that average accuracy would obscure. These findings have a clear audience among researchers studying visual robustness and learned invariance.

The experimental design controls the total number of object identities and training images while varying orientation coverage. Five repetitions with randomized instance assignments and reported variability strengthen the behavioral evidence.

The experiments cover three object families, multiple training orientation ranges, several architectures, and transfer across categories. Pretraining, rotation augmentation, and reduced-data controls provide useful corroboration within the studied setting.

The basic experimental setup and geometric components are understandable, and the heatmaps effectively connect object appearance with recognition performance. Code and data links support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Necessary clarification and validation: The partition underlying the neural analysis is not reproducibly specified. Section 2.5 defines generalizable orientations by f_w exceeding 10% of its maximum, but Equation 4 is an uncalibrated sum of sigmoid outputs fitted using Pearson correlation. Figure S9c displays scores approximately between 1.8 and 2.5; applying the stated threshold to that range would classify every displayed orientation as generalizable. Specify any missing normalization or correct the threshold, and verify the partitions used in Figures 5 and S8. This affects central evidence, rather than merely presentation.

Necessary claim correction: Figure 5 establishes associations between accuracy and activation statistics, but does not establish that invariance transfers from fully-seen to partially-seen objects through shared feature-selective neurons. Common sensitivity to image appearance could also produce these associations. Although the abstract appropriately introduces a hypothesis, Sections 3.3–4 make stronger claims that generalization is driven by this mechanism and that biological recognition mechanisms largely apply to DNNs. Consistently restrict these statements to a supported hypothesis, or provide targeted interventions that distinguish the proposed mechanism from alternatives.

Necessary measurement qualification: Equations 5–7 compare mean activations across orientation sets. Equal means can yield maximal measured invariance despite substantial variation across individual orientations, so this statistic alone does not establish individual-neuron orientation invariance. Moreover, averaging only pairs exceeding the activity threshold can select different neuron–instance subsets across conditions. Report orientation-level variability, retained-pair counts, and threshold sensitivity, or narrow the interpretation to similarity of selected mean responses.

Necessary distinction between fitting and prediction: Section 2.4 optimizes the same Pearson correlation subsequently presented as predictive performance in Figures 4 and S5, without describing a held-out evaluation. The strong correlations support the geometric model as a compact descriptive fit; they do not establish its ability to predict an unseen experiment from its training orientation range. Specify the fitting/evaluation split and provide held-out validation if retaining that stronger claim, or consistently describe the results as goodness of fit.

Optional improvements: Enlarge the dense supplementary figure labels and tabulate important correlations with uncertainty. Additional lighting, background, or natural-image experiments would improve external validity, but are not prerequisites for publishing appropriately bounded conclusions about this supervised rendered-object setting.
